lessons.title: Pipes: Pass It Along!
lessons.description: Use a pipe to pass things from one command to another.

slides.title: Meet the pipe: |
slides.body:
Imagine a little toy train carrying blocks. The pipe symbol `|` is the track that carries things from one command to the next.

The command on the left sends. The command on the right gets the things.

slides.title: Send, then sort
slides.body: First, ask for some pretend animal names. Then pass them through the pipe to sort them A to Z.
slides.explain: Think: Get the animal names -> pass them along -> put them in order. These are teaching examples, like pretend play.

slides.title: Let only some things through
slides.body: A filter is like choosing only the red blocks from a big pile. `Where-Object` lets matching things pass.
slides.explain: Think: Get the colors -> let only Red through.

slides.title: More than one stop
slides.body: A pipe train can visit more than one command. Each command does one small job, then passes the things along.
slides.explain: Get animal names -> sort them -> show the first two.

slides.title: Your turn: send it along!
slides.body: Can you spot the pipe? Say what happens first, and what happens next.
slides.explain: First we get the toy names. The pipe passes them to Sort-Object, which puts them in order. This is a pretend teaching example, not a command supported by the simulator.

lessons.title: Variables: Labeled Toy Boxes
lessons.description: Give a value a name so you can use it again.

slides.title: A name for your things
slides.body:
A variable is like a toy box with a label. Put something in the box, and its name helps you find it again.

In PowerShell, variable names start with `$`.

slides.title: Make a labeled box
slides.body: The equals sign puts a value into the box. Here, `$pet` is the label and `Bunny` is what goes inside.
slides.explain: Read it like: Put Bunny in the box named pet. This is a teaching example; variables are not supported in the simulator yet.

slides.title: Use the box again
slides.body: When you use `$pet`, PowerShell knows you mean the value inside the pet box.
slides.explain: This would show Bunny. The `$` means 'look inside this named box.'

slides.title: You can change what's inside
slides.body: Put a new value in the same box, and the old value is replaced.
slides.explain: Now the pet box holds Kitten, so using `$pet` shows Kitten.

slides.title: Your turn: name a snack!
slides.body: What snack would you put in a box called `$snack`? Try changing the example value.
slides.explain: The box named snack holds Apple. Using `$snack` asks for the value inside. This is a teaching example; variables are not supported in the simulator yet.

lessons.title: Commands: Little Helpers
lessons.description: A command is a helper that does a job when you ask.

slides.title: Ask a helper
slides.body: A command is like asking a helper to do one job. PowerShell commands often have a doing word and a thing word.

slides.title: Find the things
slides.body: `Get-ChildItem` asks to see the things in your pretend workspace.
slides.explain: Get means find or show. ChildItem means the items inside this place. The simulator shows virtual workspace items.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Try asking to see the workspace items.
slides.explain: This supported command lists items in the virtual workspace.

slides.title: A folder is a room
slides.body: Imagine your files are toys. A folder is a room where you keep some toys together.

slides.title: Make a room
slides.body: Use `New-Item` to make a folder in the virtual workspace.
slides.explain: This makes a folder named Toys inside PowerShellish's pretend workspace.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Make a room called Drawings.
slides.explain: This creates a virtual folder. It does not make a folder on your computer.

lessons.title: Files: Little Notebooks
lessons.description: Create a text file in your workspace.

slides.title: A file is a notebook
slides.body: A text file is like a little notebook. You can give it a name and write words inside.

slides.title: Make a notebook
slides.body: Let's make an empty note called hello.txt.
slides.explain: This creates a text file in the virtual workspace.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Make a note called my-story.txt.
slides.explain: The file lives in the virtual workspace. You can see it with Get-ChildItem.

lessons.title: File Words: Make a Sandwich
lessons.description: Put words into a file and read them back.

slides.title: Put words inside
slides.body: A file is like a sandwich bag. `Set-Content` puts words in. `Get-Content` takes a peek inside.

slides.title: Write a message
slides.body: Use `-Path` to name the file and `-Value` to say what goes inside.
slides.explain: This writes Hello, friend! into hello.txt in the virtual workspace.

slides.title: Read your note
slides.body: Now ask to see the words in hello.txt.
slides.explain: This reads the text from your virtual file.

lessons.title: Parameters: Helpful Labels
lessons.description: Parameters give a command extra details.

slides.title: Add a label
slides.body: A command can need a little more information. A parameter is like a label on a lunchbox telling us what's inside.

slides.title: Tell it which file
slides.body: `-Path` is a label that tells the command which file to use.
slides.explain: Get-Content reads. -Path hello.txt tells it which virtual file to read.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Change the file name to read a different note.
slides.explain: The value after -Path is the file name. This works when that file exists in your workspace.

lessons.title: Search: Play Hide and Seek
lessons.description: Find words inside a file with Select-String.

slides.title: Find the hidden word
slides.body: Searching a file is like looking for one word in a big story. `Select-String` can look for a word in text.

slides.title: Look for a word
slides.body: Give the search a word and a file to look in.
slides.explain: This looks for the word friend in hello.txt. This command is a teaching example and may not run in the simulator.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Pick a word you wrote in a file and look for it.
slides.explain: Pattern is the word to find. This example teaches PowerShell syntax; search is not supported by every simulator command set.

lessons.title: Sort: Tidy the Toy Shelf
lessons.description: Put a list in a helpful order.

slides.title: Put things in order
slides.body: Sorting is like lining up toys from smallest to biggest, or names from A to Z.

slides.title: Sort the names
slides.body: `Sort-Object` puts the items it receives into order.
slides.explain: Get the virtual workspace items, pass them along, then sort by name.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Try sorting your workspace items by name.
slides.explain: The pipe passes the listed items to the sorter.

lessons.title: Export: Pack a Copy
lessons.description: Download a copy of a workspace file to keep.

slides.title: Pack your work
slides.body: Exporting is like packing a copy of your work into your backpack so you can keep it outside the pretend workspace.

slides.title: Download one file
slides.body: `Export-File` downloads a copy of a file from the virtual workspace.
slides.explain: This downloads hello.txt to your device. It does not run a native PowerShell command.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: If hello.txt exists, download a copy to keep.
slides.explain: Exporting gives you a copy you can keep. Download your work regularly.

lessons.title: Add-Content: Add Another Block
lessons.description: Add new words after the words already in a file.

slides.title: Keep building
slides.body: `Set-Content` replaces what's in a file. `Add-Content` is like adding another block to your tower: the old words stay, and new words go at the end.

slides.title: Add one more line
slides.body: Use `-Value` to say what new words to add.
slides.explain: This adds See you soon! after the text already in the virtual file.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Add a friendly line to hello.txt.
slides.explain: Add-Content keeps the old words and adds these new ones.

lessons.title: Rename: Give It a New Name
lessons.description: Change the name of a workspace file or folder.

slides.title: A new name tag
slides.body: Sometimes a toy's name tag needs changing. `Rename-Item` gives a virtual file or folder a new name.

slides.title: Change the file name
slides.body: Tell PowerShell the current path and the new name.
slides.explain: This renames hello.txt to welcome.txt in the virtual workspace.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: If my-story.txt exists, give it the name story.txt.
slides.explain: Rename-Item changes the name in your virtual workspace.

lessons.title: Get-Help: Ask for a Map
lessons.description: Ask for help when you want to learn a command.

slides.title: It's okay to ask
slides.body: When you don't know what a command does, asking for help is a smart next step. It's like asking for a map when you're exploring.

slides.title: Show help topics
slides.body: Ask `Get-Help` to show the help topics available in PowerShellish.
slides.explain: Get-Help is available in this simulator and introduces commands and lessons.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Open the help topics in the terminal.
slides.explain: You can ask for help whenever you need a reminder.

lessons.title: Quotes: Keep Words Together
lessons.description: Use quotes to show where your text begins and ends.

slides.title: Put words in a bubble
slides.body: Quotes are like a speech bubble around words. They show PowerShell which words belong together as one piece of text.

slides.title: Write a whole message
slides.body: Put quotes around the message you want to save.
slides.explain: Everything between the quotes is one message. Set-Content writes it in the virtual file.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.body: Change the message inside the quotes to something you like.
slides.explain: Keep the opening and closing quotes so the words stay together.

lessons.title: Remove-Item: Ask Before Tidying
lessons.description: Learn that deleting needs care and confirmation.

slides.title: Check before it goes
slides.body: Deleting is like putting a drawing in the recycling bin. Stop and check first, because you may want it later.

slides.title: The command asks first
slides.body: In PowerShellish, `Remove-Item` shows an in-app confirmation before it removes a virtual item.
slides.explain: The confirmation gives you a chance to cancel. This only removes an item from the virtual workspace.

slides.title: Your turn: look before removing
slides.body: Try the command only if you really want to remove hello.txt. Read the confirmation carefully.
slides.explain: You can cancel at the confirmation. Removing a folder also removes the items inside it.
